description: Fast travel as a WORLD-SIMULATION operation (US-3 and US-4 of 122-traversal-and-travel), and the part of this module a generic engine cannot supply: every engine can already put a character somewhere else, and none of them can say what the world did meanwhile. Each case carries the WHOLE input — the authored link graph, the traveller’s modes, the runtime closures, the seed, the journey ordinal, and the fully resolved FastTravelTuning and TraversalTuning — so a harness in any language reproduces it with no defaults table, no world file and no KB. `expected.route` is the route the journey is PRICED from, found by the same uniform-cost search a walk uses, which is why a landslide on the only pass refuses the journey too: you cannot fast travel past something you could not have walked past, and a case pins exactly that with `plan: null`. `expected.plan.hours` is the route cost times the world’s `hoursPerCost`, floored, clamped up to `minimumHours` and down to `ceiling`; `ceiling` is the SMALLER of `maxHours` and `stepHours × maxSteps`, because the two bound different things — how much the world moves, and how many times the dependent systems are woken to move it — and cases pin both winning. A journey longer than the ceiling is truncated and reported `capped`, never refused. `plan.steps` are the bounded advances, summing to `hours` exactly with the last one carrying the remainder, each with a `draw` in [0, 1) derived from (seed, actor, from, to, journey ordinal, step index) and rounded to four places — never a shared RNG advanced per step, so the same journey later in the same playthrough draws different numbers and a replay reproduces both. `plan.cost` is what walking it WOULD have cost and is deliberately not charged: a journey spends TIME, and a simulation that passed a day and a half and emptied the meter has charged for the trip twice. There is no journey predicate and no elapsed fact — what a fast travel does to the world is that the CLOCK moved and everything downstream of it ran, so `expected.arrival` and `expected.discovery` are the only deltas and both are in predicates that already existed. Regenerate with `npm run traversal-corpus`.

cases.name: a-journey-passes-the-world-time-the-route-costs
cases.note: THE case the mechanic exists for. A fast travel is not a teleport: the route to the ridge costs 30 out of the shared meter, the world’s `hoursPerCost` turns that into 30 hours, and the journey is broken into five six-hour advances the dependent systems run FORWARD through — so a shop that opens in the middle of the trip is open when it should be. An implementation that hands the clock one 30-hour jump reproduces the elapsed total and gets every schedule inside it wrong.

cases.name: the-same-journey-later-in-the-playthrough-draws-different-numbers
cases.note: Every draw is derived from (seed, actor, from, to, journey ordinal, step index) and from nothing else — never a shared RNG advanced once per step, which would make the schedule depend on how many journeys ran before it. The identical trip as the playthrough’s FOURTH journey has the same hours and the same step boundaries and different draws, which is what lets an ambush on the road be stochastic and still reproducible. The journey ordinal is why it rides in the save.

cases.name: a-trip-next-door-still-takes-the-authored-minimum
cases.note: `minimumHours` clamps up, and here the world prices travel at a tenth of an hour per unit so the four-cost walk to the ford floors to zero. A journey that passed no time at all would be a teleport with extra steps, so it takes an hour and the world lives through it.

cases.name: a-journey-longer-than-the-ceiling-is-truncated-and-says-so
cases.note: The answer to "can a long journey hang the game". A world that prices travel at ten hours per unit wants 250 hours for this route; the ceiling is 72, so the advance is truncated to it, `capped` is true and the trip runs twelve advances rather than forty-two. Arriving late is a better answer than a destination the player cannot reach, so it is never refused.

cases.name: the-ceiling-is-the-smaller-of-the-two-authored-bounds
cases.note: Bounded TWICE, because the two bounds bound different things and a game needs both: `maxHours` bounds how much the world moves, and `stepHours × maxSteps` bounds how many times the dependent systems are woken to move it. Here the world authors a generous 100 hours and a budget of four advances, so the step budget wins at 24 and the number is reported on the plan rather than living in a source file. A port that implements only `maxHours` runs a 100-hour journey here.

cases.name: the-last-advance-carries-the-remainder-and-the-steps-sum-to-the-hours
cases.note: Twenty-five hours in six-hour advances is 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 1, not five sixes and an overshoot. The steps always sum to the elapsed total exactly, which is what makes the elapsed world an honest function of the journey rather than of the step size — and the caller has already clamped the hours to the ceiling, which is what makes that possible.

cases.name: a-journey-along-a-conditional-route-carries-the-goal-the-rules-layer-answers
cases.note: The only route to the ridge without the jump goes through the water, so the plan carries the rope goal of the leg that asks it, deduplicated and in route order. Core cannot evaluate an authored Prolog goal, so a journey is refused `requires` by the decision layer and not here — and it is evaluated by the pack’s own `traversal_goal_met/2`, which rebinds the goal to the caller’s actor.

cases.name: a-world-that-authored-travel-as-instantaneous-runs-no-advance-at-all
cases.note: The honest zero. A world whose `hoursPerCost` and `minimumHours` are both zero produces a plan with no steps, so nothing is advanced and the traveller simply arrives — and it is still a decision, still gated on discovery and permissibility, and still priced from a route the actor could have walked. A port that runs one advance "because there is always one" wakes every dependent system for a journey the world said takes no time.

cases.name: negative-a-landslide-on-the-only-pass-refuses-the-journey-too
cases.note: THE negative case, and the whole reason this is a world operation rather than a menu that ignores the world. The route is found by the same `reachable/3` a walk uses, so closing the two ways across the water leaves no route and there is NO PLAN — not a plan at zero hours, and not an arrival. You cannot fast travel past something you could not have walked past. An implementation that teleports to any discovered place passes every other case in this file.

cases.name: negative-a-mode-the-traveller-does-not-have-is-a-destination-they-cannot-reach
cases.note: The second negative, on a different mechanism: nothing is closed, the graph is whole, and the traveller can only walk. Every way across the water needs a mode they do not have, so there is no route and no plan. Reachability is the actor’s, not the map’s.
